Even as a child, I always found this [scene in "Bill and Ted's Excellent Adventure"](https://youtu.be/ywbJvbUj9qw?si=IaK4xqTjPN_-Uklg) where they accidentally stop by the future to be strangely moving. 

I also think this [scene from "Cool Runnings"](https://youtu.be/tYRtTqx-IK8?si=WArG8MAR7CcQtpqs), has a rare profoundness that you see from any movie period, on its insight into the nature of happiness and contentment, and how getting exactly what you want isn't an automatic assurance of that.

I really love the moment in Hot Rod when Kevin shows Rod the stunt compilation video he's been making. Rod genuinely looks super gassed about it and Kevin (despite still being embarrassed) seems really proud that Rod likes it.

Napoleon Dynamite has a few scenes like this, but the prom scene in particular gets me every time. The movie is pretty earnest about the budding relationship between Napoleon and Deb, and they have a sweet moment of connection here. Neither of them know how to express themselves, so Napoleon compliments her sleeves and asks how her glamour shots are going, and Deb invites him to a private photo shoot some time. She looks so happy here, and is just realizing that Napoleon might be her "person." Very pure and relatable. 

And then we get this gorgeous, 20 second shot where the camera slowly zooms out from Napoleon & Deb, revealing the whole scene of the gloriously 80's prom around them while "Time After Time," the perfect soundtrack choice here, swells in the background. I genuinely think this is a beautifully composed shot, from the colorful outfits and disco lights, to the way it underlines the significance of this core relationship in the movie. 

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y4aCZcVvLdE

I legitimately think Walk Hard is a masterpiece.  There are a lot of genre parodies out there, but not many of them are as carefully made as Walk Hard.  John C Reilly is a fantastic singer as well as being a fantastic comedy actor, which is a rare combination, and allows for a movie like this to actually get made in the first place.  It hits every note of musical biopics in such a perfect way that exposes the formula so perfectly with a silliness that a lot of parodies don't come close to.

And for it to end on a song like that is just amazing and shoes such a mastery of tone.

Read this oral history article if you want a long and interesting breakdown of what the actors and writers were thinking when they made it.  It's clearly very carefully made.  Its also funny how Jenna Fischer reveals how sexy she found John C Reilly.

[https://www.theringer.com/movies/2019/5/29/18642513/walk-hard-dewey-cox-oral-history-john-c-reilly-music-biopic-jake-kasdan-judd-apatow](https://www.theringer.com/movies/2019/5/29/18642513/walk-hard-dewey-cox-oral-history-john-c-reilly-music-biopic-jake-kasdan-judd-apatow)

Jacques Tati did this a lot. His comedies were some of the few that crossed the line into cinematic art. Try Mon Oncle; it’s not exactly your definition, but Tati’s imagination was consistently silly yet contemplative, and both traits relied on his acute observational skills.

Other examples:
- Clerks
- Crime Wave (not the Sam Raimi one, but still from 1985)
- In Bruges

You might be able to find more examples in Charlie Chaplin films.

The ManEater song/scene in "No Hard Feelings" was amazing and (for me at least) entirely unexpected.

Not really one moment, but for me the main character of Annie in Bridesmaids is unnecessarily tragic for such a broad comedy. What she's going through is too real, too depressing. And her story isn't really resolved. She just says 'I'll be OK' - but given her choices and actions up to that point it's not all that believable that suddenly her life is going to turn around just because it's the end of the movie. There's no reason why Annie will be OK, and the film low key let's the audience know this. In an earlier scene Annie herself argues that people don't really change. Bridesmaids is one of my favourite comedies, but I know a few people who don't like it, and one the reasons they give is the character of Annie is too real and sad.
The ending of Happiness of the Katakuris with the grandfather and granddaughter was actually surprisingly touching to me, and that movie is one of the silliest/most insane movies of all time
